intro_html: Vindaloo came to Goa with Portuguese sailors as a dish of pork preserved in wine and garlic, and Indian cooks turned the wine into vinegar and the garlic into a proper spice paste. That vinegar is what makes vindaloo taste like nothing else on an Indian menu. It is sharp and hot and deep all at once, not just hot. Each bowl carries 566 calories and 52 grams of protein for about $3.78 a serving (at everyday cost).
cost_closing_html: About $3.78 a bowl (at everyday cost). Dried chiles are the biggest line, and they are also the item that goes furthest, because a bag of them will still be in your pantry long after this batch is a memory.
shop_smart: Make the paste yourself. Jarred vindaloo paste costs several dollars a jar and tastes muted next to soaked dried chiles blended with garlic, ginger, and vinegar. This is the whole dish and it takes ten minutes.

Dried chiles are sold in bags that will cover many, many batches. Buy them from the Hispanic aisle rather than the tiny spice jars in the baking section, where the same product costs several times as much per ounce.
Boneless thighs are the recommended cut. Vindaloo is a hard simmer with acid in it, and breast meat turns to string under those conditions.
Whole spices like cumin and coriander are cheaper ground at home and taste dramatically better. If you have a coffee grinder you never use for coffee anymore, this is its second career.
make_it: Weigh your empty mixing pot and write the number down for portioning later.
Soak the dried chiles in hot water for 20 minutes until they soften, then drain and reserve some of the soaking liquid.

Blend the soaked chiles with the garlic, ginger, white vinegar, lime juice, dijon mustard, coriander, cumin, cinnamon, turmeric, garam masala, salt, and sugar into a smooth paste. Add soaking liquid until the blender moves. Taste it and brace yourself, because it is meant to be intense at this stage.
Cut the chicken thighs into large pieces and toss them with about a third of the paste. Let them sit at least an hour in the fridge.

Heat the vegetable oil in a heavy pot and cook the sliced onions slowly until they go deep golden brown, about 20 minutes. This is where the sweetness that balances the vinegar comes from, so do not stop at pale yellow.
Add the rest of the paste and fry it in the oil for 5 minutes, stirring, until it darkens and the oil separates out at the edges.
Add the chicken with its marinade and the tomato sauce, bring it to a simmer, and cook uncovered 30 to 35 minutes until the chicken is tender and the sauce clings.
Taste for salt and vinegar. Vindaloo should finish sharp, so add a splash more vinegar if it has gone flat.
portion_html: Set the full pot on the scale, subtract the empty-pot weight you wrote down, and divide by 14. Stir well before scooping so every container gets the same ratio of chicken to sauce. Each portion lands at 566 calories, and vindaloo is one of those dishes that is genuinely better on day three once the vinegar has settled in.

steps: Soak the dried chiles in hot water until soft.
Blend the chiles with garlic, ginger, vinegar, lime juice, mustard, and spices into a smooth paste.
Marinate the cut chicken thighs in a third of the paste for an hour.
Brown the onions deeply, then fry the remaining paste until the oil separates.
Add the chicken and tomato sauce and simmer uncovered 30 to 35 minutes.
Adjust the vinegar, then weigh the pot and divide into 14 containers.
